candidates.quote: Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought.
candidates.author: John Rawls
candidates.locator: Chapter I, section 1, p. 3 (Harvard University Press, 1971)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the first sentence of the century's central book on justice, and it tells a reader before breakfast that fairness is not decoration on an institution but the thing that makes it worth having.

candidates.quote: Act in such a way that you always treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never simply as a means, but always at the same time as an end.
candidates.author: Immanuel Kant
candidates.work: Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals
candidates.locator: Second Section, Academy 4:429 (in The Moral Law, Hutchinson, 1948)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The formula of humanity is the plainest rule anyone can carry into a working day: no one you deal with today is only a means to your errand. Kant stands at two for the year, so landing him closes him.

candidates.quote: Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains.
candidates.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
candidates.locator: Book I, chapter 1, the opening sentence
candidates.whyThisMonth: It opens the month with the grievance that every argument about what is owed begins from, and it is a summons rather than a lament: Rousseau spends the rest of the book asking what would make the bond legitimate.

candidates.quote: Injustice brings about the ruin of civilization.
candidates.author: Ibn Khaldun
candidates.locator: Chapter III, section 41, the section heading (Bollingen, 1958)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A fourteenth-century historian makes justice a practical matter rather than a sentiment: take from people and they stop building, which is a bracing thought at six. Note honestly that the sentence is Rosenthal's printed section heading, not a sentence lifted from the body of the chapter.

candidates.quote: There is no wealth but life.
candidates.author: John Ruskin
candidates.locator: Essay IV, Ad Valorem (Smith, Elder, 1862); first in Cornhill Magazine, 1860
candidates.whyThisMonth: Five words that reset what a day of work is for, from the book that turned political economy into a question of what people are owed. Ruskin stands at one for the year, in a different work.

candidates.quote: In the happiness of his subjects lies his happiness; in their welfare his welfare; whatever pleases himself he shall not consider as good, but whatever pleases his subjects he shall consider as good.
candidates.author: Kautilya
candidates.locator: Book I, chapter XIX, The Duties of a King (trans. Bangalore Government Press, 1915)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest manual of statecraft in the list says the person in charge is paid in other people's welfare, which is the definition of service anyone with a team can use by nine. Dating and authorship of the text are traditional and disputed, and the note should say so.

candidates.quote: Justice is a habit whereby a man renders to each one his due by a constant and perpetual will.
candidates.author: Thomas Aquinas
candidates.locator: Secunda Secundae, question 58, article 1, the reply (Burns Oates and Washbourne, 1920)
candidates.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province, 1920
candidates.whyThisMonth: The standard definition of the word the month is built on, and the useful part is habit: justice is something practised daily, not felt once. Aquinas is restating the Roman jurists' formula and endorsing it, which the note should carry.

candidates.quote: My final prayer: O my body, make of me always a man who questions!
candidates.author: Frantz Fanon
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last line of the book, and it asks for the one habit justice actually needs from a reader at six in the morning: to keep asking rather than to settle.

candidates.quote: What is wanted for women is equal rights, equal admission to all social privileges; not a position apart, a sort of sentimental priesthood.
candidates.author: Harriet Taylor Mill
candidates.locator: Westminster and Foreign Quarterly Review, July 1851, near the close, on the Worcester convention resolutions
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence refuses flattery in place of fairness, which is exactly the trade a reader is offered all day; it also names the difference between being admired and being admitted.

candidates.quote: Woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights.
candidates.author: Olympe de Gouges
candidates.work: Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen
candidates.locator: Article I (in The French Revolution and Human Rights, Bedford, 1996, pp. 124 to 129)
candidates.whyThisMonth: One woman answered the Declaration of the Rights of Man article by article, and the first article is the whole month in eleven words: what is owed is owed to everyone or it is not owed at all.

candidates.quote: We are the only animal species in which the female depends on the male for food, the only animal species in which the sex-relation is also an economic relation.
candidates.author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the argument the book is known by, and it makes a moral question out of an arrangement everyone had agreed to stop noticing, which is what a justice month is for.

candidates.quote: Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently.
candidates.author: Rosa Luxemburg
candidates.locator: Chapter 6, The Problem of Dictatorship (Workers Age Publishers, 1940)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The test of a fair room is how it treats the person who disagrees, and a reader can apply that before the first meeting of the day. Written in 1918 and first printed in 1922; in Luxemburg's manuscript the sentence stands in a footnote, which the note should say. She stands at one for the year.

candidates.quote: I know you do not make the laws, but I also know that you are the wives and mothers, the sisters and daughters of those who do; and if you really suppose you can do nothing to overthrow slavery, you are greatly mistaken.
candidates.author: Angelina Grimké
candidates.work: Appeal to the Christian Women of the South
candidates.locator: The passage answering why women are appealed to (American Anti-Slavery Society, 1836)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It closes the exit a reader reaches for first, that having no power means having no part; Grimké names the institution without describing any cruelty, so it stays publishable. Her sister Sarah already stands in the year, and they are different persons.

candidates.quote: Caring involves stepping out of one’s own personal frame of reference into the other’s.
candidates.author: Nel Noddings
candidates.work: Caring: A Feminine Approach to Ethics and Moral Education
candidates.whyThisMonth: The founding definition of care ethics, and it gives the service half of the month something a reader can actually do at six: start from the other person's view, not from your own good intentions.

candidates.quote: The notion of obligations comes before that of rights, which is subordinate and relative to the former.
candidates.author: Simone Weil
candidates.locator: Part One, the opening sentence (Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1952)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The opening sentence of the book, and the exact hinge of a month called what is owed: it turns the reader from what they are due to what they owe. Weil stands at two for the year, so landing her closes her.

candidates.quote: Your silence will not protect you.
candidates.author: Audre Lorde
candidates.locator: The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action, p. 41 (The Crossing Press, 1984)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Six words that put the cost of keeping quiet where a reader can feel it before the day starts. Flag the risk honestly: the piece was first delivered as a panel paper in December 1977 and printed in 1978, so a verifier may rule it the Makers' ground rather than an essay.
